brand-vs-ingredient: Tylenol is the name a company gave the product; the **ingredient** that does the work is acetaminophen. The same ingredient is in other brands, and **cold medicines like Panpyrin, Pancol and Theraflu contain 300–650 mg each**. That's why “I didn't take any Tylenol” while taking a cold medicine is the most common overdose accident. Checking the **ingredient name** on the back of the box is half of staying safe.
fever-not-cure: Fever reducers control symptoms — they don't cure

A fever reducer just lowers the fever for a while to make you comfortable; it **doesn't remove the cause (such as an infection)**. So a fever coming down doesn't mean you're better, and the cause can grow while you get by on fever reducers. **If a fever lasts more than 3 days, comes back after going down, or a child is limp**, don't buy more medicine — get the cause checked.
one-nsaid: Only one anti-inflammatory at a time

Ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin, Geborin (isopropylantipyrine) and prescription anti-inflammatories (aceclofenac and others) are all **the same class**. They block the same enzyme, so doubling up barely adds pain relief, but **the amount in your body doubles**. The strain on your stomach and kidneys **grows with the dose.** If you want more pain relief, take acetaminophen — a different class — **together** with it; there's evidence this combination works better than either alone. The label for **Penzal** (ethenzamide) says not to take it with other pain relievers or cold medicines. It also contains acetaminophen and so overlaps with Tylenol — when you take Penzal, take it alone.
tid: What ‘3 times a day after meals’ means

‘3 times a day, 30 minutes after meals’ on a prescription means **30 minutes after breakfast, lunch and dinner**, roughly **8 hours apart**. Don't skip the medicine because you skipped a meal — take it with milk or a snack (anti-inflammatories should not be taken on an empty stomach). If you forget once, take it as soon as you remember, but if the next dose is near, skip it and **don't take a double dose**.
apap-total: Acetaminophen: 4 g a day is the limit

That's eight 500 mg tablets. The 4 g counts **everything combined**, including acetaminophen in cold medicines, combination painkillers and sleep aids; for people 65 or older, who drink often, or who weigh little, clinicians recommend 3 g or less (the label has no age limit, so talk to a doctor or pharmacist). Going over this line damages the liver, and it's more dangerous because there are no symptoms at first.
elderly: Older adults: remember just three things

① Anti-inflammatories **with a stomach protector, and short-term** — after 65 the risks of stomach bleeding and kidney strain rise. ② **Cold medicines, sleep aids and motion-sickness pills** (first-generation antihistamines) cause dizziness, falls and trouble urinating, so avoid them where possible. ③ **Write your medicines on one page** and show it at the pharmacy and clinic — My medicines in this app is that page.
two-names: Medicines have two names. The **ingredient name** is the real name, the same everywhere in the world; the **brand name** is a nickname the company gives it. One ingredient, acetaminophen, carries many nicknames such as Tylenol. To see whether a hospital prescription and a pharmacy purchase overlap, check the **ingredient name on the back of the box**. Different names with the same ingredient mean you're taking a double dose.
expiry: The date on the box is for an **unopened** pack. Once opened, it's much shorter. Powders and liquid medicines are usually good for **a month**, eye drops **a month** after opening, and single-use artificial tears should be thrown away **the same day**. Dispensed medicine was prescribed for that illness, so don't take leftovers next time you have similar symptoms. If it changes color, smells, or tablets crumble, throw it away whatever the date.
storage: Most medicines are best kept in **a cool, dry place out of the light**. Two mistakes are common. First, **the bathroom shelf** — humidity and temperature swings make medicine spoil fastest there. Second, **throwing away the original box** — it shows the expiry date and ingredients. Some syrups need refrigeration and some don't, so check the label. Put leftover medicine in a **pharmacy medicine-disposal bin**, not the trash.
with-water: Taking medicine with drinks other than water can change how it works. **Grapefruit juice** blocks the breakdown of many medicines and can raise levels dangerously. **Milk and antacids** block absorption of some antibiotics and osteoporosis medicines. **Green and black tea** reduce iron absorption. **Alcohol** interacts badly with almost every medicine — with acetaminophen it strains the liver, with anti-inflammatories the stomach. Take a full glass of water, and don't lie down right after swallowing.
cut-pill: Can I cut a tablet in half?

**If there's a score line down the middle**, it's made to be cut, so you can. If there's no line, don't. In particular, tablets named **‘extended-release, ER, CR or XR’** are made to release slowly all day; cutting or chewing them can release a whole day's dose at once, which can be dangerous. Opening capsules to take just the powder shouldn't be done lightly for the same reason. If swallowing is hard, ask your pharmacist whether there's **a syrup with the same ingredient or a product that can be cut**.
missed-dose: There's one rule. **Take it as soon as you remember, but skip it if your next dose is near.** Never take a double dose. If you forget the evening dose of a three-times-a-day medicine, just let it go and carry on from the next morning. But **taking antibiotics on and off is the worst** — the medicine can't build up enough to kill the bacteria, and the bacteria just get used to it. Keep to the set days and times, and if you want to stop early, don't stop on your own — ask your prescriber. If you often forget, set a reminder.
before-after-meal: Why some medicines are before or after meals

**After meals** is usually to protect the stomach — medicines hard on the stomach, like anti-inflammatories, belong here. **30 minutes before meals** is for medicines whose absorption food interferes with, or that need to work before you eat — such as acid reducers and some diabetes medicines. **On an empty stomach (1 hour before or 2 hours after a meal)** is for medicines that hardly absorb at all with food; thyroid and osteoporosis medicines are typical. If unsure, follow what's written on the bag, and if nothing is written, ask your pharmacist.
antibiotics: Antibiotics: finish as directed, never for colds

Antibiotics kill **bacteria**. Colds and flu are **viruses**, so antibiotics don't work on them. Taking them anyway only kills the good bacteria in your body, causing diarrhea, and next time you really need them they may not work. **Keep to the prescribed days.** But the old explanation that “stopping midway makes bacteria stronger” isn't well supported — these days **shorter courses from the start** are thought to reduce resistance. So if you feel better with days left, **don't stop on your own — ask your prescriber.** Some illnesses can be treated briefly, while others, like tuberculosis, must be treated for a long time. And **keeping leftover antibiotics to take next time** is the most common and dangerous habit — the bacteria then and now differ, and too small a dose only breeds resistance.
steroid-fear: Steroids aren't something only to fear

Steroids are very powerful at putting out inflammation. Older adults often fear them as ‘bone-melting drugs’, but **the problems come from taking them for a long time or applying them widely for a long time**. Applying to the skin for a few days or an occasional joint injection is usually safe. On the other hand, **using them carelessly for long periods** really does cause trouble — steroid on athlete's foot spreads the fungus, and long use on the face thins the skin. The keys are **keeping to the period your doctor set** and **not stopping oral steroids suddenly**.
polypharmacy: If you take more than five medicines

Getting medicines from several clinics can lead to the same ingredient doubling up or medicines clashing. Older adults especially can have **drowsiness, dizziness, constipation and trouble urinating** pile up and lead to falls. Once a year, **put all your medicines in one bag** and show them to a doctor or pharmacist. This is called a medication review, and more medicines can be stopped than you'd think. Register them in My medicines in this app and we'll tell you automatically when ingredients overlap.
generic: No. A generic is approved **only if it has the same ingredient and strength as the original and passes a test showing the body absorbs the same amount (bioequivalence)**. It's cheaper because there were no development costs, not because it's inferior. Color, shape and size may differ, though, so people are often surprised when the same medicine looks different after changing clinic or pharmacy. In that case, just check that **the ingredient name is the same**.
supplement-not-drug: Health supplements **fill in what's missing**; they don't cure illness. But some act like medicines, so take care. **Omega-3 and ginkgo** have been reported to increase bleeding with blood thinners, so tell your doctor or pharmacist; **calcium, iron and magnesium** block absorption of thyroid medicine and some antibiotics. If you're having surgery, **tell them a week before**. And taking a multivitamin together with single supplements makes it easy to exceed upper limits.
elderly-caution: Medicines older adults should be especially careful with

With age, the kidneys and liver process medicines more slowly, so **the same dose acts more strongly**. Be especially careful with these. **Drowsy cold medicines, sleep aids and motion-sickness pills** (antihistamines) bring dizziness, trouble urinating and falls. **Anti-inflammatories** carry much higher risks of stomach bleeding and kidney strain than in younger years. **Muscle relaxants** cause drowsiness that makes falls more likely. That's why acetaminophen and medicines applied to the skin are suggested first for older adults. If you feel dizzy or foggy after a new medicine, don't put up with it — tell someone.
when-er: Call 119 instead of taking medicine when…

Some signs mean you shouldn't get by on medicine. **Crushing chest pain with cold sweat** (heart attack), **slurred speech or weakness in one arm or leg** (stroke), **the worst headache of your life**, **shortness of breath with blue lips**, **vomiting blood or black stools**, **confusion or drowsiness**. With strokes and heart attacks especially, **time decides the lasting damage**. If in doubt, don't wait — call 119. It's fine if it turns out to be nothing — better than being late.
antibiotic-when: When antibiotics are needed — and when they're not

**They're not needed** far more often. They don't work for colds, most sore throats and coughs, runny noses, viral stomach bugs or eye infections. **They may be needed** for throat infections with white patches on the tonsils and fever, yellow nasal discharge with facial pain lasting more than ten days (sinusitis), ear infections with pus, red spreading skin infections, and bladder infections with painful, frequent urination. Asking **“Do I really need an antibiotic?”** at your visit isn't rude — it's a good question.
diarrhea-water: With diarrhea, fluids come before anti-diarrhea medicine

What makes a stomach bug dangerous isn't the diarrhea itself but **dehydration**. So the core of treatment is **oral rehydration solution**, not anti-diarrhea medicine. Plain water alone dilutes your salts, and sports drinks are sugary and can worsen diarrhea. Drink pharmacy rehydration solution **chilled, in small sips often**. And **don't use anti-diarrhea medicine for diarrhea with fever or blood** — it traps the germs in the gut. Rather than counting bowel movements, watch **whether you're passing urine well**.
hand-wash: For stomach bugs and eye infections, handwashing prevents spread more reliably than any medicine. How you do it matters. **Norovirus isn't killed well by alcohol hand sanitizer.** Wash with soap under running water for 30 seconds, including between fingers and under nails. Pink eye also spreads by hand. Use separate towels and pillowcases and change them often. Simply **not cooking for the family** while you're sick can stop the whole household from falling ill.
fever-vs-infection: Not every fever means a bacterial infection

A fever is a sign your body is fighting, not proof of a bacterial infection. Viruses like colds, flu and stomach bugs cause fevers too. So **fever ≠ antibiotics**. Instead, look at **what comes with it**: white patches on the tonsils, yellow phlegm with shortness of breath, pain when urinating with flank pain, red spreading skin, a stiff neck — when these come together you need to be seen. And **a fever lasting more than 3 days** needs checking whatever the cause.
probiotic-timing: Take probiotics 2 hours apart from antibiotics

Antibiotics can't pick out only bad bacteria, so the good bacteria in your gut decrease too. That's why diarrhea is common. There's evidence that probiotics (especially Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG and Saccharomyces boulardii) reduce this diarrhea. Bacterial probiotics are usually taken **about 2 hours apart from the antibiotic** (Saccharomyces boulardii is a yeast and isn't affected by antibiotics), and taking them for 1–2 weeks after finishing the antibiotic helps your gut recover faster.
read-label: Three things to check on the pharmacy bag

A prescription bag shows three things. **One, the ingredient name** — check here whether it overlaps with what you bought at the pharmacy. **Two, when and how often** — before or after meals, how many times a day. **Three, how many days** — antibiotics must be taken for the full number of days. Don't throw the bag away; keep it until you finish. Taking a photo lets you show it as is at another clinic, which is much safer.
pharmacist-swap: When the pharmacist says “This one is better”

Pharmacists may **suggest something better** based on stock and your condition. It's usually well meant. But if you don't know the ingredient name, you just take what you're given. There's only one thing to check — **“Is this the same ingredient as what I was looking for?”** If it is, any product is fine; if not, ask **“What is this medicine for?”** If the price differs a lot, you can ask why. In Yakjido, just enter the suggested medicine's name and we'll **check right away whether it's the same medicine**.
grapefruit: Grapefruit (and its juice) blocks an enzyme the liver uses to break down medicines, so some medicines act **much stronger than the dose taken**. Well-known examples are **some cholesterol medicines (simvastatin, atorvastatin, lovastatin)**, **some blood pressure medicines (calcium channel blockers like nifedipine and felodipine)**, and some sleeping pills and heart-rhythm medicines. Some, like rosuvastatin and pravastatin, are fine — if your bag lists one of the affected ingredients, avoid grapefruit; oranges and tangerines are OK. One glass can have effects lasting more than a day, so **spacing the timing doesn't solve it.**
warfarin-food: Warfarin works against vitamin K. Suddenly eating a lot of vitamin K–rich foods like spinach, kale, broccoli, **natto and cheonggukjang** weakens it, and suddenly stopping makes it stronger. The answer is **not to cut them out but to eat a similar amount each week**. On the other hand, **ginkgo, high-dose omega-3, red ginseng and cranberry juice** can shift your clotting levels, so talk to your doctor before starting them. If your gums or nose bleed often or bruises get bigger, it's time to check your levels.
coffee-meds: Coffee and medicines: three things that happen together

① **Iron supplements** taken with coffee or tea are absorbed less than half as well — keep them 2 hours apart. ② **Caffeine in cold medicines and pain relievers** (the Penzal and Geborin types) plus coffee brings palpitations and sleeplessness. ③ **The asthma medicine theophylline and some antibiotics (quinolones)** block caffeine breakdown, so one cup of coffee acts like two or three. If coffee feels unusually strong while you're on a medicine, suspect that combination.
blood-donate: Before donating blood — some medicines mean you can't

Even if you're healthy, **the medicines you take** can mean you can't donate for a while, because the ingredient may pass to the person receiving the blood. The rules are set in Korea's **Blood Management Act Enforcement Rules (persons barred from donating)**. Three common ones: · **Aspirin** — within 3 days of taking it, you can't give **platelet donations** · **Acne medicine (isotretinoin) and hair-loss medicine (finasteride)** — **1 month** after the last dose · **Prostate and hair-loss medicine (dutasteride)** — **6 months** after the last dose. If you've had growth hormone or insulin from cattle, or used immunosuppressants, the wait can be much longer or donation may not be possible. **The surest way is to tell the blood donation center the exact names of your medicines.** You can also show your pharmacy bag or My medicines in this app. Hiding it puts the person receiving the blood at risk. ※ Source: Blood Management Act Enforcement Rules (persons barred from donating) · Korean Red Cross Blood Services. Many medicines aren't listed here, so the rule is to **name your medicines exactly at the screening interview**.
blood-ask: At the hospital, mention the ‘medicines you take’ first

Before surgery, procedures, endoscopy, tooth extraction, or when planning a pregnancy, the first thing the care team asks is **what medicines you're taking now**. Be sure to mention these in particular: · **Blood thinners** (aspirin, anticoagulants) — you may need to stop them a few days before a procedure · **Anti-inflammatory painkillers** — they can increase bleeding · **Diabetes and blood pressure medicines** — what to do on fasting days is decided separately · **Supplements and herbal medicines** — easy to leave out because they don't seem like medicine, but some affect blood and the liver. **Don't stop on your own.** Stopping is also for the care team to decide. Just ask, “Can I keep taking this medicine?”
stop-danger: Some medicines are dangerous to stop on your own

Many people stop medicines themselves because they feel better or it seems like too many. Most medicines can be stopped safely, but a few **get worse than before if stopped suddenly**. · **Blood pressure medicine** — blood pressure can spike higher than before. Well-controlled pressure means the medicine is working, not that you're cured · **Steroids (by mouth)** — if taken for more than 2 weeks, your body's own production is resting. Stopping suddenly causes weakness and low blood pressure. Always taper off · **Blood thinners (aspirin, clopidogrel, warfarin, etc.)** — if taken after a stent or stroke, stopping raises the risk of a blockage right away · **Thyroid hormone and diabetes medicines** — levels quietly worsen, and symptoms appear only much later · **Depression/anxiety medicines and sleeping pills** — stopping suddenly causes dizziness, sleeplessness and tingling. There's a tapering schedule · **Epilepsy and Parkinson's medicines** — seizures or stiffness can occur. **Wanting to cut down is a good thought in itself.** Just don't stop alone — at your next visit, say **“Could I reduce this medicine?”** Many medicines do need reducing with age. If you suspect a side effect and want to stop right away, it's safest to stop and then call your prescriber **the same day**.
patch-howto: How to apply pain-relief patches so they itch less

A patch puts anti-inflammatory medicine right where it hurts, so its biggest advantage is **almost no strain on the stomach or heart**. Instead, skin problems are common. **Tips** · **Wash and dry the area** before applying. Leftover lotion stops it sticking and increases irritation · **Don't keep applying to the same spot.** Moving it a little each time greatly reduces itching · You don't need to wear it all day. **Wear for 8–12 hours, then give the skin a rest** · Don't apply on wounds, eczema or sunburned skin. **Ketoprofen (Ketotop and others) has one more point** — it can make skin red and blistered when exposed to sunlight. So Korea's drug regulator added **not for under 15** and **keep the area covered from sunlight for 2 weeks after removal** to the label. The rash can appear after removing the patch, so the cause is easily missed. **If you've had a rash after using sunscreen**, take extra care. Sunscreen ingredients (oxybenzone, octocrylene) and ketoprofen cross-react. So do fibrate cholesterol medicines. **If it itches, switch ingredients.** Felbinac, diclofenac, piroxicam and flurbiprofen patches are available at pharmacies without ketoprofen's “cover for 2 weeks after removal” warning (sun rashes can still rarely occur). Not all patches are the same medicine. ※ Sources: MFDS ketoprofen topical label change (2010) · photoallergic contact allergy mechanism (Karlsson 2014) · octocrylene cross-reaction (Avenel-Audran 2010)
dispose: Leftover medicine goes to the pharmacy, not the trash

**Don't throw leftover or expired medicine in the trash or toilet.** The ingredients seep into soil and water, and children or pets at home can swallow them. **Where to dispose** · **Medicine-disposal bins** at pharmacies, public health centers, community service centers and district offices · In some areas such as Seoul, you can also use **post boxes** — write **‘waste medicine’ on an envelope and seal it**. **How to pack it** · Tablets and capsules: in their packaging as is · Powders: unopened as is · Liquids and syrups: **with the cap tightly closed** (they can leak onto mail, so **use a bin, not a post box**) · Ointments and eye drops: whole, with the cap on. **Not for these bins**: health supplements like red ginseng and vitamins aren't waste medicine — they go in **general trash**. Sorting your home medicines just once a year helps. Medicines with worn-off names, or ones you can't identify, are the most dangerous. ※ Source: Seoul Metropolitan Government waste-medicine disposal guide · local household waste sorting rules. Whether post boxes accept them varies by area, so **ask your community center or pharmacy** to be sure.
patch-heat: Don't use an electric blanket over a pain-relief patch

This is the most common medicine accident for older adults in winter. **Placing an electric blanket, heating pad or hand warmer over a patch** opens the skin's blood vessels and the medicine is absorbed all at once. It can burn, then **blister like a burn**. The approved label says so too — **don't heat it; bathe 30 minutes to an hour after removing it; don't apply right after bathing.** Getting into hot water with a patch on makes irritation much stronger. And **if it's no better after five or six days of patches**, stop and get advice. Don't forget to move it a little each time instead of keeping it on the same spot. With ketoprofen patches, **the area stays sensitive to sunlight for up to 2 weeks after removal**, so keep it covered.
caffeine: Anti-drowsiness gum, energy drinks, coffee — how much caffeine a day

The ingredient that keeps you awake in anti-drowsiness gum, energy drinks and coffee is mainly **caffeine**. Anti-drowsiness gum is **food**, not medicine, so caffeine, guarana (a caffeine-containing fruit) and menthol vary by product — check the **caffeine content on the pack**. The daily maximum recommended by Korea's drug regulator is **400 mg or less for adults · 300 mg or less in pregnancy · 2.5 mg per kg of body weight or less for children and teens** (for example, 100 mg for a 40 kg student). Some **cold medicines and headache medicines (combination pain relievers) also contain caffeine**, so count them together with coffee and energy drinks. Even within the limit, cut back **if your heart races or you can't sleep**. If pregnant, have less and talk to a doctor or pharmacist.
kidney-otc: Dialysis and kidney disease — choosing pharmacy medicines

**Every time you buy medicine at a pharmacy, say first “I'm on dialysis” or “My kidneys are bad.”** Many medicines leave the body through the kidneys, so the same medicine can build up or further damage the kidney function you have left. **Don't buy — the label says not to take it** · Anti-inflammatory painkillers by mouth (ibuprofen, naproxen, etc.) — the label says not to use them in severe kidney disease. Avoid them if your kidney function number (glomerular filtration rate) is below 30. · Magnesium laxatives (Magmil) — not taken with kidney disease. · Sodium phosphate enemas (Reclean, etc.) — not used in severe kidney disease, and not without a doctor's instruction if you have kidney disease. · Nasal decongestant cold medicines with pseudoephedrine — not taken in severe kidney disease. **Ask first — the label says to consult** · Famotidine (acid reducer) — it builds up. When kidney function is very low, even prescriptions are reduced to 20 mg every other day (US label). · Antacids (Gelfos, Almagel) and Gaviscon — they contain aluminum, magnesium and sodium. Almagel isn't recommended for severe kidney impairment (label) — if you have kidney disease, talk to your doctor first. · Most combination cold medicines. **For pain or fever — acetaminophen (Tylenol) usually comes first.** In clinics, acetaminophen is used instead of anti-inflammatories even for people on dialysis. But the label says not to take it in severe kidney disease, and the US label also says to lengthen the interval and lower the daily total when kidneys are very poor. **Get the number of doses and the daily maximum set by your dialysis unit or your doctor.**
